claim: Drosophila syncytial nuclear divisions limit transcription unit size of early zygotic genes.
source: Drosophila syncytial nuclear divisions limit transcription unit size of early zygotic genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known constraint on early zygotic gene expression.

claim: Mitosis inhibits not only transcription, but also pre-mRNA splicing.
source: As mitosis inhibits not only transcription, but also pre-mRNA splicing, we reasoned that constraints on splicing were likely to exist in the early embryo
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the abstract, with citation to Shin and Manley, 2002 in the introduction.

claim: Most early zygotic genes are intronless.
source: being splicing avoidance a possible explanation why most early zygotic genes are intronless.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to De Renzis et al., 2007 in the introduction.

claim: Two mutant alleles for a subunit of the NTC/Prp19 complexes specifically impaired pre-mRNA splicing of early zygotic but not maternally encoded transcripts.
source: We isolated two mutant alleles for a subunit of the NTC/Prp19 complexes, which specifically impaired pre-mRNA splicing of early zygotic but not maternally encoded transcripts.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through RT-PCR and RNA-Seq data in Figures 2B, 2C, and 2D.

claim: Ectopic maternal expression of an early zygotic pre-mRNA was sufficient to suppress its splicing defects in the mutant background.
source: Ectopic maternal expression of an early zygotic pre-mRNA was sufficient to suppress its splicing defects in the mutant background.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5B.

claim: A small early zygotic transcript with multiple introns was poorly spliced in wild-type embryos.
source: Furthermore, a small early zygotic transcript with multiple introns was poorly spliced in wild-type embryos.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6B and 6E.

claim: There exists a developmental pre-requisite for highly efficient splicing during Drosophila early embryonic development.
source: Our findings demonstrate for the first time the existence of a developmental pre-requisite for highly efficient splicing during Drosophila early embryonic development
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Highly proliferative tissues need coordination between cell cycle and gene architecture to ensure correct gene expression and avoid abnormally processed transcripts.
source: suggest in highly proliferative tissues a need for coordination between cell cycle and gene architecture to ensure correct gene expression and avoid abnormally processed transcripts.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract, inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Drosophila embryonic development starts with thirteen nuclear divisions without cytokinesis (syncytial blastoderm).
source: Drosophila melanogaster embryonic development starts with thirteen nuclear divisions without cytokinesis (syncytial blastoderm), these divisions being among the fastest known for any animal embryonic system (Foe and Alberts, 1983).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation to Foe and Alberts, 1983.

claim: Syncytial blastoderm nuclear divisions are among the fastest known for any animal embryonic system.
source: Drosophila melanogaster embryonic development starts with thirteen nuclear divisions without cytokinesis (syncytial blastoderm), these divisions being among the fastest known for any animal embryonic system (Foe and Alberts, 1983).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation to Foe and Alberts, 1983.

claim: Drosophila syncytial blastoderm formation relies on maternally encoded gene products loaded into the egg during oogenesis.
source: Drosophila syncytial blastoderm formation relies on the maternally encoded gene products loaded into the egg during oogenesis (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009.

claim: The maternal to zygotic transition (MZT) occurs when nuclei enter interphase 14.
source: After fertilization, as nuclei enter interphase 14, the maternal to zygotic transition (MZT) occurs in which the soma suddenly becomes transcriptionally active and many of the maternally encoded gene products are rapidly degraded (Anderson and Lengyel, 1979; McKnight and Miller, 1976; Yasuda et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to Anderson and Lengyel, 1979; McKnight and Miller, 1976; Yasuda et al., 1991.

claim: There is an initial wave of zygotic gene expression during syncytial nuclear divisions 8–13.
source: While the major burst of zygotic transcription occurs once the nuclei arrest in interphase 14, there is an initial wave of zygotic gene expression during the syncytial nuclear divisions 8–13 (Pritchard and Schubiger, 1996; ten Bosch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations to Pritchard and Schubiger, 1996; ten Bosch et al., 2006.

claim: Approximately 70% of early zygotic genes are small in size and intronless.

claim: Only 20% of Drosophila genes are intronless.
source: As only 20% of Drosophila genes are intronless, it has been proposed that small intronless genes have an important selective advantage for transcription during the syncytial blastoderm formation (De Renzis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation to De Renzis et al., 2007.

claim: Pre-mRNA splicing is mostly co-transcriptional in yeast, Drosophila, and human cells.

claim: In vivo splicing rates are in the order of 30 s to approximately 3 min once the intron is transcribed.

claim: Syncytial blastoderm interphases can be as short as 4 to 5 min.

claim: Mitosis inhibits splicing.

claim: The differential splicing defects in fandango mutants were not related to differential association of spliceosomal components to the NTC/Prp19 complexes.

claim: Constraints on pre-mRNA splicing are present during Drosophila early embryonic development.

claim: The requirement for overall splicing efficiency is likely to vary during development.

claim: Only the first intron (int1) of the 4x intron kuk-LacZ construct was correctly spliced when it was zygotically expressed in wild-type embryos under the control of an endogenous early zygotic minimal promoter.
source: Only the first intron (int1) of the 4x intron kuk-LacZ construct was correctly spliced when it was zygotically expressed in wild-type embryos under the control of an endogenous early zygotic minimal promoter (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When the 4x intron kuk-LacZ construct was early zygotically expressed under the control of the inducible promoter UAS/Gal4 there were similar splicing defects (intron retention).
source: Likewise, when the 4x intron kuk-LacZ construct was early zygotically expressed under the control of the inducible promoter UAS/Gal4 there were similar splicing defects (intron retention) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Half-lives for splicing reactions are <1 min for the first intron, but 2–8 min for both second and third introns.
source: Measurement of in vivo kinetics of mRNA splicing showed that half-lives for splicing reactions are <1 min for the first intron, but 2–8 min for both second and third introns (Audibert et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Audibert et al., 2002.

claim: Splicing of two or more introns requires more time than transcription and becomes rate limiting.
source: Hence, splicing of two or more introns requires more time than transcription and becomes rate limiting.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetics data cited from Audibert et al., 2002.

claim: When the 4x intron kuk-LacZ construct was zygotically expressed, the splicing defects of the firstly transcribed 5′-localized introns (Int1 and Int2) were significantly weaker than those observed in the later transcribed 3′-localized introns (Int3 and Int4).
source: Consistent with the hypothesis of a temporal constraint on pre-mRNA splicing, when the 4x intron kuk-LacZ construct was zygotically expressed, the splicing defects of the firstly transcribed 5′-localized introns (Int1 and Int2) were significantly weaker than those observed in the later transcribed 3′-localized introns (Int3 and Int4) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Maternal expression of the 4x intron kuk-LacZ construct was sufficient to significantly suppress its splicing defects.
source: Importantly, maternal expression of this construct was sufficient to significantly suppress its splicing defects (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Real-time qPCR analysis showed that the 4x intron kuk-LacZ and no intron kuk-LacZ constructs were equivalently zygotically and maternally expressed.
source: Real-time qPCR analysis showed that these constructs were equivalently zygotically and maternally expressed (Figure 6C,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C,F.

claim: Splicing did not quantitatively impair early zygotic transcription.
source: This suggested that splicing did not quantitatively impair early zygotic transcription, which was consistent with the observation that the rates of transcriptional elongation proceed independently of splicing (Brody et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data and stated with citation to Brody et al., 2011.

claim: The rates of transcriptional elongation proceed independently of splicing.
source: This suggested that splicing did not quantitatively impair early zygotic transcription, which was consistent with the observation that the rates of transcriptional elongation proceed independently of splicing (Brody et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Brody et al., 2011.

claim: A moderate decrease in the length of syncytial blastoderm interphases (seen in grapes mutant embryos) was not sufficient to induce splicing defects in otherwise wild-type embryos.
source: Although a moderate decrease in the length of syncytial blastoderm interphases (seen in grapes mutant embryos [Sibon et al., 1997]) was not sufficient to induce splicing defects in otherwise wild-type embryos (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Sibon et al., 1997.

claim: Avoidance of pre-mRNA splicing during early zygotic expression is a consequence of the extremely short interphases and frequent mitotic cycles.
source: we hypothesize that avoidance of pre-mRNA splicing during early zygotic expression is a consequence of the extremely short interphases and frequent mitotic cycles.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the text, inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Mosquito Aedes aegypti early zygotic transcripts are frequently intronless when compared with the rest of the transcriptome.
source: Similarly to Drosophila, mosquito Aedes aegypti and the zebrafish Danio rerio early zygotic transcripts are frequently intronless when compared with the rest of the transcriptome (Biedler et al., 2012; Heyn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Biedler et al., 2012; Heyn et al., 2014.

claim: Zebrafish Danio rerio early zygotic transcripts are frequently intronless when compared with the rest of the transcriptome.
source: Similarly to Drosophila, mosquito Aedes aegypti and the zebrafish Danio rerio early zygotic transcripts are frequently intronless when compared with the rest of the transcriptome (Biedler et al., 2012; Heyn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Biedler et al., 2012; Heyn et al., 2014.

claim: Cell cycle constraints during early embryonic development are a force capable of driving changes in gene architecture of multicellular organisms.
source: Our results highlight cell cycle constraints during early embryonic development as a force capable of driving changes in gene architecture of multicellular organisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text, inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: In unicellular organisms intron paucity correlates with a bias toward the 5′ ends.
source: In unicellular organisms intron paucity correlates with a bias toward the 5′ ends, whereas introns from multicellular genomes are evenly distributed throughout the genes (Mourier and Jeffares, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Mourier and Jeffares, 2003.

claim: Introns from multicellular genomes are evenly distributed throughout the genes.
source: In unicellular organisms intron paucity correlates with a bias toward the 5′ ends, whereas introns from multicellular genomes are evenly distributed throughout the genes (Mourier and Jeffares, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Mourier and Jeffares, 2003.

claim: Similar constraints on gene architecture are likely to exist in yeast and other fast-dividing single cell eukaryotes.
source: This suggests that similar constraints on gene architecture are also likely to exist in yeast and other fast-dividing single cell eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the text, inferred from the comparison with unicellular organisms.

claim: The NTC/Prp19 complexes are known to be important for efficient spliceosome activation.
source: Since the NTC/Prp19 complexes are known to be important for efficient spliceosome activation, and our mutant alleles specifically impaired pre-mRNA splicing of early zygotic but not maternally encoded transcripts, we propose that overall requirements for splicing efficiency are likely to vary during development, being the NTC/Prp19 complexes a key modulator of spliceosome activation rates.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Overall requirements for splicing efficiency are likely to vary during development, being the NTC/Prp19 complexes a key modulator of spliceosome activation rates.
source: Since the NTC/Prp19 complexes are known to be important for efficient spliceosome activation, and our mutant alleles specifically impaired pre-mRNA splicing of early zygotic but not maternally encoded transcripts, we propose that overall requirements for splicing efficiency are likely to vary during development, being the NTC/Prp19 complexes a key modulator of spliceosome activation rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text, inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Prp19 expression varies during neuronal differentiation.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, Prp19 expression varies during neuronal differentiation (Urano et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Urano et al., 2006.

claim: In plants, removal of retained introns regulates translation in rapidly developing gametophytes.
source: In plants it was recently shown that removal of retained introns regulates translation in rapidly developing gametophytes (Boothby et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Boothby et al., 2013.

claim: A sub-population of early zygotic transcripts with introns showed some degree of intron retention in wild-type embryos.
source: In Drosophila, a sub-population of early zygotic transcripts with introns similarly showed some degree of intron retention in wild-type embryos (Figure 2B,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The pre-requisite for highly efficient splicing during early embryonic development is paradoxically also likely to play an important regulatory role in the expression of a subset of early zygotic transcripts.
source: Our results also suggest that the pre-requisite for highly efficient splicing during early embryonic development is paradoxically also likely to play an important regulatory role in the expression of a subset of early zygotic transcripts, which further supports the possibility that modulation of spliceosome activation per se is important for differential regulation of gene expression during development.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text, inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Modulation of spliceosome activation per se is important for differential regulation of gene expression during development.
source: Our results also suggest that the pre-requisite for highly efficient splicing during early embryonic development is paradoxically also likely to play an important regulatory role in the expression of a subset of early zygotic transcripts, which further supports the possibility that modulation of spliceosome activation per se is important for differential regulation of gene expression during development.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the text, inferred from the experimental findings.
